PHSCS 587

Band energy and potential

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows why rising electrostatic potential bends electron bands downward

Band diagrams track electron energy; voltmeters track differences in electrostatic potential or electrochemical conditions. If material parameters are uniform, a local electrostatic potential ψ shifts an electron’s potential energy by −qψ. Thus EC(x) = EC0 − qψ(x), and EV shifts by the same amount when the bandgap remains fixed.

The electric field is Efield = −dψ/dx in one dimension. With EC measured in joules, Efield = (1/q)dEC/dx. A conduction electron experiences force −qEfield, while a hole experiences +qEfield. If energies are plotted numerically in eV, a one-volt potential increase lowers an electron band energy by one eV; keep the unit conversion explicit in derivatives.

A flat equilibrium Fermi level can coexist with curved EC and EV. Carrier concentration gradients then accompany the electrostatic field, and drift and diffusion balance to give zero net equilibrium current. Band bending alone does not establish a current without occupancy and boundary conditions.

Example

Moving from ψ = 0 to ψ = +0.2 V lowers electron potential energy by 0.2 eV. The associated field direction depends on which spatial direction has the increasing ψ.

Practice

1. If EC slopes upward with increasing x, which way does the electric field point?

Use Efield = (1/q)dEC/dx with q positive.

The field points toward +x. An electron’s electrostatic force points toward −x.
